title: Three major cue-sport cultures
context: The next detail page can compare three rule families: British snooker, American 9-ball pool and Chinese heyball. These cultures connect geography, broadcast format, table equipment and player identity.

players.name: United Kingdom
honors: Crucible Theatre became the symbolic home of modern snooker
Colour TV made red-colour patterns and long tactical frames watchable
anecdotes: The 1985 black-ball final became a reference point for how TV could turn snooker into national drama.
players.note: Use this region as the bridge into snooker rules: large table, many reds, tactical safety and break-building.

players.name: United States
players.eraRole: Fast rotation pool and tournament showdowns
honors: U.S. Open 9-Ball and Mosconi Cup shaped modern American pool identity
American pool culture prizes break power, run-outs and pressure racks
anecdotes: The Mosconi Cup turned USA vs Europe into a yearly team-rivalry format with crowd noise closer to darts than snooker.
players.note: Use this region as the bridge into 9-ball rules: rotation order, break control, safeties and hill-hill pressure.

players.name: China
players.eraRole: Hybrid table, mass participation and fast-growing prize events
honors: Heyball entered the WPA international structure and is being promoted globally
Large Chinese events have helped make the discipline commercially visible
anecdotes: The game is useful educationally because it looks familiar to pool players but punishes them with tighter, snooker-like potting demands.
players.note: Use this region as the bridge into Chinese 8-ball rules: hybrid equipment, solids/stripes structure and regional identity.

title: Television made snooker visible
context: Colour television and BBC programming made snooker easy to follow at home. This generation turned tactical safety play, long matches and player personalities into mass entertainment.

players.name: Steve Davis
honors: Six UK Championships and three Masters titles
First officially recognised televised competitive 147 in 1982
anecdotes: Known as The Nugget, Davis became the face of snooker's 1980s TV boom.
His rivalry era culminated culturally in the 1985 black-ball final against Dennis Taylor.
players.note: Davis represented the first fully modern television-era professional: disciplined, repeatable and commercially marketable.

players.name: Alex Higgins
anecdotes: His 1982 World Championship semi-final clearance against Jimmy White is still treated as a mythic TV moment.
He helped sell snooker as drama, not only precision.
players.note: Higgins is important for culture even when compared with later title totals.

players.name: Jimmy White
anecdotes: White's repeated Crucible near-misses made him one of the sport's most loved TV figures.
The 1994 final against Hendry turned a missed black into one of snooker's most painful stories.
players.note: White is useful as a card about popularity: he shows that cultural impact is not only measured by world titles.

title: The break-building revolution
context: Stephen Hendry changed what elite snooker looked like: aggressive long potting, early frame-winning breaks and a champion's refusal to play only containment.

players.name: Stephen Hendry
honors: Five UK Championships and six Masters titles
Youngest World Champion at 21 years 106 days
anecdotes: Hendry's ten-frame burst against Jimmy White in the 1992 final became a symbol of his killer instinct.
He made one-visit snooker the new elite standard.
players.note: Hendry forced the next generation to become more attacking.

players.name: John Parrott
anecdotes: Parrott beat Jimmy White 18-11 in the 1991 world final.
He later became a familiar BBC studio presence, extending his cultural role beyond playing.
players.note: Parrott was an important early-1990s figure before Hendry's dominance became overwhelming.

players.name: Ken Doherty
honors: Reached finals in all three Triple Crown events
anecdotes: Doherty ended Hendry's World Championship reign in the 1997 final.
His nickname The Darling of Dublin captured his role as Ireland's major snooker figure.
players.note: Doherty broadened the champion map beyond Britain and showed that defensive craft still mattered.

title: The long-lived superstars
context: Ronnie O'Sullivan, John Higgins and Mark Williams turned professional in 1992 and remained relevant for decades. Their contrast is useful for player cards: genius speed, all-round craft and natural potting.

players.name: Ronnie O'Sullivan
anecdotes: His 1997 Crucible 147 is remembered as the fastest maximum in professional snooker.
His personality card should feel different: genius, volatility, honesty and theatre are part of the brand.
players.note: O'Sullivan became the sport's global reference point: talent, speed, longevity and public attention in one figure.

players.name: John Higgins
anecdotes: The Masters deciding-frame clearance against O'Sullivan in 2006 is a classic pressure example.
Higgins is often the teaching model for complete snooker, not just spectacular snooker.
players.note: Higgins is often used as the model for complete snooker: scoring, safety, cue-ball control and match IQ.

players.name: Mark Williams
honors: Completed the Triple Crown in the 2002/03 season
One of the greatest natural potters
anecdotes: His 2018 World Championship comeback title came 15 years after his previous world crown.
His relaxed public persona contrasts with extraordinary pressure potting.
players.note: Williams' laid-back style makes him a strong contrast card against the more intense Higgins and Hendry archetypes.

title: American 9-ball and global pool icons
context: 9-ball culture is faster, louder and more rack-based than snooker. The American line is important, but modern pool is also Filipino, Taiwanese, European and increasingly international.

players.name: Efren Reyes
honors: First player to win world titles in two pool disciplines
anecdotes: Nicknamed The Magician because he regularly found escape routes other players did not see.
His 1994 U.S. Open 9-Ball win over Earl Strickland introduced many American fans to Filipino pool greatness.
players.note: Reyes is essential for explaining pool culture as artistry and problem-solving, not just potting.

players.name: Earl Strickland
anecdotes: Strickland is associated with one of pool's most famous run-out stories: an 11-rack package in 1996.
His rivalry and contrast with Efren Reyes is perfect for a culture card: American fire vs Filipino imagination.
players.note: Use Earl to show that American pool is partly sport, partly showmanship.

players.name: Shane Van Boening
anecdotes: Known as The South Dakota Kid, he comes from a pool-playing family.
His deafness is often framed not as a limitation but as part of his extraordinary visual concentration.
players.note: Van Boening is the cleanest bridge from classic American pool to the modern Matchroom era.

players.name: Fedor Gorst
honors: Mosconi Cup winner with Team Europe
anecdotes: Gorst switched from Russian pyramid to American pool as a child.
His second world 9-ball title made him one of the youngest multiple world champions in pool.
players.note: Gorst shows the new professional pool archetype: global, technical, data-aware and extremely consistent.

title: Snooker globalisation and China's first wave
context: After the TV boom, snooker became a global product. Ding Junhui's 2005 China Open win created a mass Chinese audience, while Marco Fu, Liang Wenbo and Neil Robertson showed that elite snooker was no longer only British.

players.name: Ding Junhui
honors: First Asian player to reach the World Championship final
anecdotes: His 2005 China Open win over Stephen Hendry was watched by a huge Chinese TV audience.
Ding became the player many later Chinese professionals named as their model.
players.note: Ding is the key card for China's first snooker wave.

players.name: Marco Fu
honors: Reached at least the semi-final stage of all three Triple Crown events
Hong Kong's most successful snooker player
anecdotes: Fu reached a ranking final as the world number 337 at the 1998 Grand Prix.
His career helps show that Chinese-language snooker culture was not only mainland China.
players.note: Fu made Hong Kong a visible part of the professional snooker map before mainland China's deeper player pipeline matured.

players.name: Liang Wenbo
honors: World Cup winner with Ding Junhui
anecdotes: Liang was one of the first mainland Chinese players many UK viewers saw deep in major events.
His card needs an integrity note: WPBSA issued him a lifetime ban in 2023.
players.note: Historically relevant to China's first wave, but present with context rather than celebration.

players.name: Neil Robertson
honors: First player to compile over 100 centuries in a season
anecdotes: Robertson became the first Australian Crucible world champion.
His 2013/14 century record is useful for showing how modern scoring volume exploded.
players.note: Robertson is the clearest example of the post-TV game's reach beyond Britain and China.

title: Chinese 8-ball / Heyball stars
context: Heyball grew from China's domestic billiards market and is now being internationalised through WPA and JOY events. Its player culture is different from snooker: more table-running, more hybrid equipment, more mass-participation identity.

players.name: Zheng Yubo
honors: Multiple JOY World Heyball Masters titles
Important name in domestic Chinese 8-ball culture
anecdotes: Zheng's name is often one of the first attached to Chinese 8-ball when fans discuss the discipline's domestic stars.
He is useful for explaining why heyball should not be treated as a small side game in China.
players.note: Use Zheng as the first heyball player card, then add more verified domestic stats as sources are collected.

players.name: Chu Bingjie
honors: Defeated Zhang Taiyi 21-19 in the 2025 final
anecdotes: Chu's 2025 International Open win came soon after Zhang Taiyi's World Games form, making the final a useful new-era rivalry card.
The reported top prize of RMB 2 million shows the commercial scale of elite heyball in China.
players.note: Chu gives the site a current heyball anchor rather than only historical Chinese snooker names.

players.name: Pan Xiaoting
honors: One of China's most recognised cue-sport athletes
Helped make billiards visible to a wider Chinese audience
anecdotes: Pan is often remembered as a bridge between competitive achievement and mainstream celebrity visibility in China.
She helps prevent the player page from becoming male-only and snooker-only.
players.note: Use Pan to connect Chinese billiards culture with women's professional pool.

players.name: Gareth Potts
honors: One of the best-known non-Chinese heyball specialists
anecdotes: Potts helps show that heyball is not only a Chinese domestic game; it is being exported back toward the UK and global pool scene.
His success is useful for comparing British cue-sport roots with China's new rule family.
players.note: Potts is a bridge card between UK billiards heritage and Chinese heyball's internationalisation.

title: Tactical pressure vs high-speed scoring
context: The 2010s split the elite snooker game into vivid styles: Selby's suffocating match play, Trump's attacking scoring, Robertson's century machine and a new group of world champions.

players.name: Mark Selby
honors: One of the best match players of the modern era
anecdotes: Selby is nicknamed The Jester from Leicester, but his table style is usually anything but light-hearted for opponents.
He is the best card for explaining why snooker is not only potting.
players.note: Selby turns frames into endurance tests.

players.name: Judd Trump
honors: First player to make 100 competitive centuries in a season
anecdotes: Trump's shot selection made modern snooker feel more clip-friendly for digital audiences.
His nickname The Ace in the Pack fits the card-game language of the site.
players.note: Trump modernised the visual appeal of snooker for short clips and fast digital audiences.

players.name: Kyren Wilson
anecdotes: Wilson's 2024 title made him the post-Class-of-92 English world champion to watch.
His card works well as a stamina-and-structure archetype.
players.note: Wilson is useful as a transition card between the 1992 class and newer champions.

players.name: Luca Brecel
anecdotes: Brecel's 2023 run included dramatic comebacks and helped widen snooker's champion geography.
His free-flowing game contrasts strongly with Selby's control style.
players.note: Brecel's 2023 title showed that the sport's champion geography had widened again.

title: China's second wave becomes championship force
context: The newest Chinese snooker generation is no longer just inspired by Ding; it is winning the biggest events. Zhao Xintong and Wu Yize make the strongest visual story for a second Chinese wave.

players.name: Zhao Xintong
anecdotes: Zhao became the first Chinese and first Asian player to win the World Championship.
His card should mention the comeback context after his 2023 suspension, because it is part of the modern story.
players.note: Zhao's 2025 title changed the Chinese snooker story from expectation to achievement.

players.name: Wu Yize
anecdotes: Wu won the 2026 world final 18-17 against Shaun Murphy in a deciding frame.
His win made Chinese world titles repeatable rather than a one-off Zhao moment.
players.note: Wu's 2026 Crucible win made the second-wave story much stronger.

players.name: Si Jiahui
anecdotes: Si's 2023 Crucible run made him a symbol of the coming Chinese generation before the world titles arrived.
His game is a good card for explaining promise, not only completed honours.
players.note: Si is a strong supporting card for the Chinese pipeline.

players.name: Xiao Guodong
anecdotes: Xiao helps show China's rise is broad: not only teenage prodigies, but also mature professionals breaking through.
His domestic event success connects elite achievement to Chinese host cities.
players.note: Xiao broadens the new-wave story beyond Zhao and Wu.
